subject: internet-basics
question: What is the Internet, in simple terms?
options: A global network of interconnected computers that can share information
A single website owned by one company
The same thing as the World Wide Web, with no difference at all
A type of computer hardware
explanation: The Internet is the physical and logical network connecting billions of devices worldwide. It's the infrastructure that things like the Web, email, and apps run on top of.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is the difference between 'the Internet' and 'the World Wide Web'?
options: The Internet is the network infrastructure; the Web is a service (websites/pages) that runs on top of it
They are exactly the same thing
The Web is older than the Internet
The Internet only refers to email
explanation: The Internet is the underlying global network. The World Wide Web is one of many services built on it — email, video calls, and file transfer are other services that also use the Internet but aren't 'the Web.'

subject: internet-basics
question: What is a web browser?
options: Software used to access and display websites, like Chrome, Firefox, or Safari
The company that owns the Internet
A type of computer virus
A physical cable that connects to the router
explanation: A browser is the application you use to request and display web pages. Common examples include Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does it mean to 'bookmark' a page in a browser?
options: Save a shortcut to that page so you can revisit it quickly later
Permanently delete the page from the internet
Report the page as spam
Download the entire website to your device
explanation: Bookmarking saves a link to a page in your browser for quick access later, without needing to search for it again or remember the exact URL.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does 'URL' stand for?
options: Uniform Resource Locator
Universal Router Link
Unique Response Language
United Resource List
explanation: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator — it's the full address used to find a specific resource (page, image, file) on the web.

subject: internet-basics
question: In the URL https://www.example.com/products, what is 'example.com' called?
options: The domain name
The protocol
The file extension
The IP address
explanation: 'example.com' is the domain name — the human-readable address that identifies a specific website, which gets translated to an IP address behind the scenes by DNS.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does the 'S' in HTTPS stand for, and why does it matter?
options: Secure — it means the connection between you and the site is encrypted
Simple — it means the site loads faster
Standard — it means the site follows web design rules
Server — it means the site has its own server
explanation: HTTPS encrypts the data traveling between your browser and the website, protecting things like passwords and payment details from being intercepted. Always prefer HTTPS sites, especially for logins or payments.

subject: internet-basics
question: You're about to enter your password on a site whose address bar shows 'Not Secure' with plain http://. What should you do?
options: Be cautious — avoid entering sensitive information, since the connection isn't encrypted
Proceed normally, it makes no difference
Enter your password twice to be extra safe
The warning only applies to online banking, not other logins
explanation: A 'Not Secure' warning on http:// means your data could be intercepted in transit. Treat this as a signal to be cautious about what information you submit on that page.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is an IP address?
options: A unique number that identifies a device on a network
A password used to log into websites
The name of your Internet browser
A type of computer virus
explanation: An IP (Internet Protocol) address is a numerical label assigned to each device connected to a network, allowing devices to find and communicate with each other.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does DNS do?
options: Translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses computers use
Encrypts your internet traffic
Blocks pop-up advertisements
Speeds up your internet connection
explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) acts like the internet's phone book — it converts domain names people type into the numerical IP addresses computers actually use to route traffic.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is an ISP?
options: Internet Service Provider — a company that provides your connection to the internet
Internal System Processor — a part of your computer's hardware
Internet Security Protocol — a type of antivirus software
International Software Program — a category of apps
explanation: An ISP (Internet Service Provider) is the company you pay for your internet connection, such as a cable, fiber, or mobile data provider.

subject: internet-basics
question: What's a key difference between Wi-Fi and mobile data?
options: Wi-Fi typically connects through a local router/network; mobile data connects directly through your carrier's cellular network
Wi-Fi only works on desktop computers
Mobile data is always faster than Wi-Fi
They are exactly the same technology
explanation: Wi-Fi relies on a nearby router (often connected via an ISP), while mobile data connects your device directly to your carrier's cell towers — useful when you're away from a Wi-Fi network.

subject: internet-basics
question: Why should you be cautious using public Wi-Fi (like at a cafe or airport) for sensitive tasks like banking?
options: Public networks are often less secure, making it easier for others on the same network to intercept your data
Public Wi-Fi is always slower, so it doesn't matter
Public Wi-Fi doesn't work with banking apps
There is no real risk — this is a myth
explanation: Open, shared networks often lack the protections of a private home network, making certain kinds of data interception easier. It's safer to avoid sensitive logins or use a trusted VPN on public Wi-Fi.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does 'bandwidth' refer to in an internet connection?
options: The amount of data that can be transferred over the connection in a given time
The physical length of the network cable
The number of devices allowed to connect
The brand of your router
explanation: Bandwidth measures data transfer capacity (often in Mbps — megabits per second). Higher bandwidth generally means faster downloads/uploads and better performance for things like video streaming.

subject: internet-basics
question: What's the difference between downloading and uploading?
options: Downloading brings data from the internet to your device; uploading sends data from your device to the internet
They are two names for the exact same action
Downloading only applies to videos; uploading only applies to photos
Uploading is always faster than downloading
explanation: Downloading = receiving data (e.g., saving a file to your phone). Uploading = sending data (e.g., posting a photo). Most home internet plans have different download and upload speeds.

subject: internet-basics
question: What are the three main parts of a typical email address, using 'name@example.com' as an example?
options: The username (name), the @ symbol, and the domain (example.com)
The subject line, the body, and the signature
The sender, the receiver, and the timestamp
The inbox, the outbox, and the spam folder
explanation: An email address has a username, the @ symbol separating it from the domain, and the domain that hosts the mailbox — similar structure to a postal address with a name and a location.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is the difference between 'CC' and 'BCC' when sending an email?
options: CC recipients are visible to everyone; BCC recipients are hidden from other recipients
CC is for attachments; BCC is for the message body
They are the same, just different names
CC is only for internal company emails
explanation: CC (carbon copy) recipients can see who else received the email. BCC (blind carbon copy) recipients are hidden — other recipients won't know they were included.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is a search engine?
options: A tool that helps you find information across the web by searching an index of pages
A type of computer virus
A device that speeds up your internet connection
A social media platform
explanation: Search engines like Google or Bing crawl and index billions of pages, letting you search for relevant content using keywords instead of knowing exact web addresses.

subject: internet-basics
question: You want more precise search results for an exact phrase. What's an effective technique?
options: Put the exact phrase in quotation marks, e.g. "free Web3 courses"
Type the query entirely in capital letters
Add as many unrelated keywords as possible
Search engines can't be made more precise
explanation: Quotation marks tell most search engines to match that exact phrase, rather than treating each word independently — a simple but powerful way to narrow results.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is 'cloud storage'?
options: Saving files on remote servers accessed over the internet, instead of only on your local device
A weather forecasting service
A type of computer virus protection
Storage that only works when it's raining, metaphorically
explanation: Cloud storage (like Google Drive or Dropbox) keeps your files on remote servers, letting you access them from multiple devices anywhere with internet access, and often provides backup benefits.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does a file extension like '.pdf' or '.jpg' tell you?
options: The type/format of the file, which determines what program is needed to open it
The exact size of the file in megabytes
The date the file was created
The owner of the file
explanation: The extension after the dot indicates the file format — .pdf for documents, .jpg for images, .mp4 for video, etc. — which tells your device (and you) what kind of app can open it.

subject: internet-basics
question: Why might a scammer disguise a malicious file as something like 'invoice.pdf.exe'?
options: To trick you into thinking it's a harmless document when it's actually an executable program
Because .exe files are always safe
Because double extensions make files load faster
This isn't a real technique used by scammers
explanation: Some systems hide the true (last) extension by default, so a file ending in '.pdf.exe' might display as just 'invoice.pdf' — tricking users into running a program instead of opening a document. Always check full file names carefully.

subject: internet-basics
question: What are browser 'cookies'?
options: Small pieces of data websites store on your device to remember information like login state or preferences
Malware that infects your computer
A snack you can order through certain websites
The cache of images your browser downloads
explanation: Cookies are small text files websites save in your browser to remember things like whether you're logged in, items in a shopping cart, or site preferences. They're normal, but can also be used for tracking.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is the benefit of using multiple browser tabs instead of multiple separate windows?
options: Tabs let you keep several pages open within one window, making it easier to switch between them without cluttering your screen
Tabs use significantly more device memory than separate windows
There is no difference at all
Tabs only work on mobile devices
explanation: Tabs let you organize multiple open pages within a single browser window, which is generally more space-efficient and easier to manage than juggling many separate windows.

subject: internet-basics
question: What's an important safety consideration before installing a browser extension?
options: Check what permissions it requests and only install extensions from trustworthy sources — some can read everything you type or browse
All extensions are automatically safe since browsers review every single one perfectly
Extensions can't access any of your browsing data
You should install as many extensions as possible for convenience
explanation: Some browser extensions request broad permissions (like reading all page content), which could be misused to capture sensitive data. Only install extensions you trust, and review their requested permissions.

subject: internet-basics
question: Why are software and browser updates important?
options: They often include security fixes that patch vulnerabilities attackers could otherwise exploit
Updates exist only to add new visual themes
Updates always make your device slower with no other benefit
Updates are optional and never contain anything important
explanation: Software updates frequently patch known security vulnerabilities. Delaying updates leaves you exposed to issues that have already been fixed by the developer but not yet applied to your device.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is a 'backup,' and why does it matter?
options: A copy of your important data stored separately, so you don't lose everything if your device is lost, damaged, or hacked
A second internet connection in case your first one fails
A type of computer virus
The recycle bin/trash folder on your device
explanation: Backups protect against data loss from device failure, theft, or ransomware — having your important files copied somewhere else (cloud or external drive) means one bad event doesn't mean losing everything.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is 'netiquette'?
options: Etiquette (polite, respectful behavior) applied to online communication
A type of network cable
A programming language
An internet speed measurement
explanation: Netiquette refers to good manners and respectful behavior in online spaces — things like not typing in all caps (which reads as shouting), staying on topic, and being considerate of others.

subject: internet-basics
question: In simple terms, what does a VPN do?
options: Creates an encrypted connection that routes your internet traffic through another server, adding privacy and security
Physically speeds up your internet connection hardware
Automatically blocks all advertisements on every site
Guarantees you can never be tracked online under any circumstances
explanation: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) encrypts your connection and routes it through another server, which can help protect data on untrusted networks (like public Wi-Fi) — though it isn't a total anonymity guarantee.

subject: internet-basics
question: Your Wi-Fi suddenly stops working. What's a reasonable first troubleshooting step?
options: Restart your router/modem, since this resolves many temporary connectivity issues
Immediately buy a new computer
Assume the entire internet is broken worldwide
Delete your browser and reinstall it
explanation: Restarting the router clears many temporary glitches and is the standard first step for connectivity issues, before assuming something more serious is wrong.

subject: internet-basics
question: A website shows '404 Error.' What does that generally mean?
options: The specific page you requested wasn't found on the server
Your internet connection is completely down
The website has been permanently shut down forever
Your device has a virus
explanation: A 404 error means the server was reached, but the specific page/resource you requested doesn't exist at that address — often due to a broken link or mistyped URL, not a broader connection problem.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is a domain name registrar?
options: A company that lets you purchase and manage ownership of a domain name
A government agency that owns the entire internet
A type of web browser
The company that manufactures your router
explanation: A domain registrar (like Namecheap or GoDaddy) is where individuals or organizations register and manage domain names, which then need to be pointed at a hosting server to actually serve a website.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does a '500 Internal Server Error' usually indicate?
options: Something went wrong on the website's own server, not with your device or connection
Your password was entered incorrectly 500 times
The website has exactly 500 pages
Your internet plan has run out of data
explanation: A 500 error is a server-side problem — the issue is on the website's end, not something wrong with your device, browser, or internet connection. Usually the best action is to try again later.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does 'IoT' (Internet of Things) refer to?
options: Everyday physical devices (like smart bulbs, thermostats, or watches) that connect to the internet
A programming language for building websites
The original name for the World Wide Web
A type of computer virus targeting smart devices
explanation: IoT refers to the growing category of physical, everyday objects — thermostats, doorbells, watches — that are connected to the internet and can send/receive data, often to make them 'smart.'

subject: internet-basics
question: What does 'streaming' mean, as in streaming a video?
options: Playing content continuously as it's delivered over the internet, rather than fully downloading it first
Permanently saving a video file to your device
Sending a video as an email attachment
A method of encrypting video files
explanation: Streaming delivers content in a continuous flow that plays as it arrives, rather than requiring the whole file to download first — this is how services like YouTube or Netflix work.

subject: internet-basics
question: You're trying to complete an online task, but your phone keeps disconnecting from Wi-Fi. Besides the router, what else is worth checking?
options: Whether Wi-Fi is actually toggled on in your device's settings and whether you're within reasonable range of the router
Whether the website you're visiting has changed its logo recently
Whether your email password has been changed
Whether your browser's bookmarks are organized correctly
explanation: Basic device-side checks — Wi-Fi toggle, airplane mode, distance from the router, or other apps hogging bandwidth — are often the actual cause, not just the router or ISP.

subject: internet-basics
question: What does 'Incognito' or 'Private Browsing' mode actually protect against?
options: It prevents your browser from saving local history/cookies for that session — it does NOT make you anonymous to websites or your ISP
It makes you completely invisible and untraceable online
It blocks your ISP from seeing any of your traffic
It automatically encrypts every website you visit
explanation: Private browsing only affects what's stored locally on your device (history, cookies) — it doesn't hide your activity from websites, your ISP, or your employer/school network. This is a common misconception worth correcting.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is 'web hosting'?
options: A service that stores a website's files on a server so it can be accessed over the internet
The process of designing a website's visual layout
A type of internet browser
The act of registering a domain name
explanation: Web hosting is the service that keeps a website's files on a server connected to the internet 24/7, so visitors can access it anytime by typing the domain name.

subject: internet-basics
question: How is a service like GitHub Pages able to host a static website for free?
options: It only serves static files (HTML/CSS/JS, no server-side processing), which is inexpensive for the provider to offer at scale as part of the platform
It secretly charges hidden fees later
It's illegal and unsustainable
It only works for exactly one day per month
explanation: Static hosting (no database or server-side code running) is relatively cheap to provide at scale, which is part of why platforms like GitHub Pages can offer it for free as a benefit of hosting your code there.

subject: internet-basics
question: A page shows 'This site can't be reached.' What's a likely cause?
options: You have no internet connection, mistyped the address, or the site's DNS couldn't be resolved
The website owner has deleted the domain name system entirely
You've been permanently banned from the internet
Your device's storage is full
explanation: This generic browser error usually points to a connectivity issue, a typo in the URL, or a DNS resolution failure — it's a good moment to double-check your internet connection and the address you typed.

subject: internet-basics
question: You receive an unexpected email with an attachment from someone you don't recognize. What's the safest approach?
options: Don't open the attachment — verify the sender through another channel first, or simply delete it
Open it immediately out of curiosity
Forward it to all your contacts to warn them, including the attachment
Reply asking them to send more attachments to confirm it's real
explanation: Unexpected attachments from unknown senders are a classic malware delivery method. When in doubt, don't open it — verify through a separate, trusted channel if you think it might be legitimate.

subject: internet-basics
question: What is a 'digital footprint'?
options: The trail of data you leave behind through your online activity — posts, searches, purchases, etc.
A type of computer keyboard shortcut
The physical size of a data center
A setting that shrinks images automatically
explanation: Every search, post, like, and purchase contributes to your digital footprint — a record of your online activity that can be seen by companies, and sometimes other people, long after you've forgotten about it.

subject: internet-basics
question: What's the difference between a 404 error and a 403 error?
options: 404 means the page wasn't found; 403 means you don't have permission to access it, even though it exists
They mean exactly the same thing
404 is a server problem; 403 is always a browser problem
403 means the site has been deleted permanently
explanation: 404 (Not Found) means the resource doesn't exist at that address. 403 (Forbidden) means the resource exists, but you're not authorized to view it — an important distinction when troubleshooting access issues.

subject: internet-basics
question: Why might streaming a lot of video use up your mobile data plan quickly?
options: Video requires transferring much more data continuously than text or simple images
Video files are always exactly 1 megabyte, regardless of length
Mobile data doesn't apply to video, only to apps
Streaming video uses no data at all if you have 'unlimited' calling
explanation: Video is data-intensive — much more so than browsing text-based pages — so streaming can consume a mobile data allowance far faster than typical browsing or messaging.

subject: internet-basics
question: A website you've never visited asks to access your camera, microphone, and location all at once. What should you consider?
options: Whether the site genuinely needs all of these for its function — deny anything that seems unnecessary or suspicious
Always click 'Allow' immediately to avoid the prompt reappearing
These prompts are purely decorative and don't actually grant access
It's impossible for a website to request this kind of access
explanation: Browser permission prompts exist precisely so you can evaluate whether a request makes sense. A simple text-based site asking for camera, mic, AND location simultaneously is worth pausing on before allowing.
